strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical extension of the HJ-RL reachability framework (Fisac et al., Hsu et al., So et al.) to two novel and practically motivated dual-objective problems, Reach-Always-Avoid and Reach-Reach, with full proofs of decomposition (Theorems 1-2), state-augmentation necessity (Fig. 2, Theorem 3), and optimality of the augmented formulation.

The decomposition results are non-trivial and elegant: reducing RAA to an avoid problem plus a modified reach-avoid problem, and RR to two reach problems plus a modified reach problem, allowing reuse of existing tractable Bellman machinery rather than requiring new solvers or heavy reward engineering as in CMDP/Lagrangian or LTL/automaton-based approaches.

The derivation is carried through to a concrete, implementable algorithm (DO-HJ-PPO) via a Stochastic Reach-Avoid Bellman Equation and policy gradient result (Proposition 1), showing the theory is not purely abstract.

Empirical validation spans a qualitative DDQN grid-world (illustrating conceptual differences from plain reach/avoid values) and quantitative continuous-control tasks (Hopper, F16) against multiple reasonably designed baselines (CPPO variants, DSTL), with consistent improvements in success rate and steps-to-success.

Good, focused positioning relative to CMDP, multi-objective RL, goal-conditioned RL, and temporal logic RL, clarifying what advantage the explicit Bellman decomposition offers over surrogate/automaton-based approaches.
weaknesses: Empirical evaluation is fairly narrow: only two continuous-control environments (Hopper, F16), no reported variance/seeds or statistical significance for the 1,000-trajectory evaluations, and no ablation study results shown for design choices explicitly claimed to matter (e.g., 'coupled resets', which the text says are critical but for which no comparison numbers are given).

The CPPO baselines (v1-v3) are custom formulations designed by the authors themselves for this comparison, which raises some concern about baseline strength/fairness; the paper itself notes CPPOv1/v2 achieve 0% success in RR, suggesting the comparison may be somewhat one-sided.

The theory assumes deterministic dynamics; the extension to the stochastic PPO setting (SRABE) is presented with much less rigor (no convergence guarantee, just an adaptation of a prior stochastic Bellman heuristic), so the gap between the clean theoretical results and the practical algorithm is not fully closed.
Scalability of the framework beyond two objectives (more than one reward/penalty pair) is not discussed, limiting understanding of the method's generality.

The main text is extremely dense/terse (reads as a compressed conference brief with proofs entirely deferred to a long supplement), which hurts self-contained readability and makes it hard to verify key claims without consulting ~15 pages of appendix proofs.

No mention of code/data release for reproducibility, and experimental details (network sizes, exact reward scaling, environment resets) are only in the supplement, making independent reproduction harder.

Related work discussion in the main text is condensed to a single paragraph, which limits contextualization of how this method compares empirically or theoretically to other safety-liveness or multi-objective reachability methods beyond the chosen baselines.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and under-explored problem: extending HJ-reachability-based RL formulations to dual-objective settings (Reach-Always-Avoid and Reach-Reach), which are more expressive than existing reach/avoid/reach-avoid formulations.

The theoretical development is extensive and rigorous, with detailed proofs (decomposition theorems, optimality of state augmentation, stochastic Bellman equation derivation, and a policy gradient proposition) provided in a lengthy supplementary material.

The decomposition idea (solving RAA/RR by composing simpler reach/avoid/reach-avoid value functions) is conceptually elegant and provides a principled bridge between the new problem classes and prior HJ-RL machinery.

The paper proposes a concrete, practical algorithm (DO-HJ-PPO) derived from the theory, including stochastic relaxations (SRABE) needed to move from idealized deterministic value functions to realistic RL settings.

Experiments span two distinct domains (a toy grid-world with DDQN for qualitative value function validation, and continuous control tasks—Hopper and F16—for the full RL algorithm), providing at least some diversity in evaluation settings.
weaknesses: The experimental section in the main text is extremely thin (roughly one page), consisting largely of qualitative description and a single composite figure, without detailed quantitative tables, confidence intervals discussion, or statistical rigor appropriate for a top-tier venue.

The baselines are weak and somewhat ad hoc: the paper itself admits CPPOv1 is the 'fairest' comparison but performs worst, while CPPOv3—described by the authors as 'naive and seemingly unfair'—is used as the strongest competing baseline, raising concerns about cherry-picking or lack of well-tuned, principled baselines.

No comparison against other reachability-based safe RL methods mentioned in related work (e.g., RESPO, RCPPO, RCPO) despite these being discussed as directly relevant prior art; CPPO and a naive STL decomposition are the only baselines actually implemented.

No ablation studies with quantitative results isolating the effect of key algorithmic design choices (e.g., coupled resets, joint vs. separate optimization of decomposed/composed objectives) — these are only discussed qualitatively/anecdotally ('we observe that omitting coupled resets causes...') without supporting numbers or figures.

The gap between the deterministic theoretical guarantees (Theorems 1-3) and the stochastic, function-approximation-based practical algorithm is acknowledged but not rigorously bridged—there is no theoretical guarantee or even empirical convergence analysis connecting SRABE/DO-HJ-PPO back to the proven optimal decomposition.

Only two continuous-control environments (Hopper, F16) are tested, both with fairly simple geometric reward/penalty structures (distance-based rewards, box/cylinder regions), limiting evidence of generality and scalability to more complex, realistic tasks.
The grid-world DDQN demonstration is purely qualitative (visual trajectories and value heatmaps) with no quantitative metrics, undermining its value as a validation of the theoretical claims.

The overall presentation is extremely dense and compressed (written like a short conference brief with nearly all substance deferred to a long appendix), which hampers clarity and makes it difficult to assess the practical contribution independent of the heavy theoretical apparatus.
No discussion of computational cost/overhead of maintaining multiple decomposed actor-critic networks relative to baselines, nor wall-clock or sample-efficiency comparisons beyond 'steps to success'.

Reproducibility is a concern: although hyperparameters are listed, no code release is mentioned, and the algorithm involves several non-trivial custom Bellman updates and coupled-reset mechanisms that would be hard to reproduce exactly from the description alone.

strengths: The paper introduces two novel and well-motivated dual-objective problem formulations (Reach-Always-Avoid and Reach-Reach) that generalize existing HJ-RL reach/avoid/reach-avoid formulations, addressing a real gap between CMDP/temporal-logic approaches and tractable Bellman-style value functions.

The theoretical contribution is substantial and rigorous: the paper provides full proofs (in the supplementary material) of decomposition theorems (Thm 1, 2) and an optimality/sufficiency result for state augmentation (Thm 3), which is a meaningful and non-trivial technical achievement.

The derivation naturally motivates a practical algorithm (DO-HJ-PPO) that extends existing SRBE/PPO machinery (from Hsu et al. and So et al.) to the new dual-objective setting with minimal modification, showing a clear theory-to-practice pipeline.

Experiments span multiple settings of increasing complexity (DDQN grid-world sanity check, then continuous control Hopper and F16), giving at least a qualitative and quantitative sense that the method behaves as intended.
The related work section clearly situates the contribution relative to CMDPs, multi-objective RL, goal-conditioned RL, and temporal logic approaches, clarifying what gap the paper aims to fill.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation in the main text is thin: results are presented only as bar-chart figures with success rate/step-count metrics, with no learning curves, variance/confidence intervals reported in text, or statistical significance testing, and the main text experimental description is only a few paragraphs long.

Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: the authors themselves describe some CPPO variants as "naive and seemingly unfair" and "non-smooth" and note CPPOv1/v2 fail entirely in RR tasks, suggesting the baselines may not have been adequately tuned or that fundamentally stronger constrained/multi-objective baselines (e.g., Lagrangian methods with better-tuned multipliers, other safe RL methods cited in related work) were not tried.

No ablation studies are provided for key algorithmic design choices beyond a brief qualitative mention that omitting "coupled resets" causes performance to degrade to baseline levels; no quantitative ablation of this or other design choices (e.g., sharing vs separate decomposed critics, choice of γ schedule) is shown.

The theory is derived under deterministic dynamics and policy assumptions, and the stochastic relaxation (SRABE) used in the final algorithm is motivated by analogy to prior work rather than fully justified theoretically for the dual-objective, continuous-action/continuous-state setting used in Hopper/F16 experiments.

The paper is extremely dense and compressed (appears to be a short-paper/brief format with most technical content relegated to a long appendix), which harms clarity and makes it difficult to assess core claims without consulting extensive supplementary proofs.

Only two continuous-control testbeds (Hopper, F16) are used, both with fairly simple/synthetic reward and penalty structures (distance-based goals and box/geofence obstacles); it's unclear how well the method would scale to higher-dimensional or more realistic safety-critical tasks.

No code or reproducibility artifacts are mentioned, which combined with the complexity of the proposed algorithm (composed and decomposed critics, coupled resets, Bellman-GAE for multiple problem types) raises reproducibility concerns.

The significance/impact of the contribution, while technically sound, appears somewhat incremental relative to the cited prior works (reach-avoid RL, SRBE/PPO), since it primarily extends decomposition results to two new but closely related composite objectives.

strengths: The paper introduces two novel and well-motivated compositional HJ-RL problems (RAA and RR) that meaningfully extend prior reach/avoid/reach-avoid formulations to dual-objective satisfaction, addressing a real gap between simple HJ-RL and full temporal-logic-based approaches.

Strong theoretical contribution: the authors rigorously prove (Theorems 1-3, with detailed appendix proofs spanning many pages) that RAA and RR values can be exactly decomposed into combinations of previously known avoid/reach/reach-avoid value functions, and prove necessity and sufficiency of state augmentation via a clean non-Markovian counterexample (Figure 3).

The paper carefully distinguishes its Bellman-value decomposition from superficially similar temporal-logic predicate algebra decompositions, with explicit counterexamples (Appendix L) showing why naive TL-style decomposition fails for value functions -- this is a nice piece of conceptual clarity.

DOHJ-PPO is a well-motivated practical algorithm with a stochastic relaxation (SRABE) justified theoretically (Theorem 4) and via policy-gradient derivation, and the coupled-reset design choice is empirically justified/ablated.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 4 diverse continuous-control environments (Hopper, F16, SafetyGym, HalfCheetah) with both RAA and RR tasks, compared against 10 baselines spanning Lagrangian, HJ-RL, STL/LTL-inspired, and MORL approaches, plus a DQN grid-world illustrative demo and a stochastic-dynamics robustness ablation.
Good related-work coverage situating the contribution relative to CMDPs, GCRL, LTL-RL, and HJ methods.
weaknesses: The main text is extremely dense and relies heavily on deferred appendix proofs; while thorough, the core theoretical exposition (Section 6) could better convey proof intuition in the main body, limiting accessibility.

DOHJ-PPO requires multiple additional actor and critic networks for decomposed objectives (Avoid/Reach-Avoid or two Reach subproblems plus composed networks), and the paper does not report additional compute/sample cost overhead relative to baselines, which matters for a claimed "little to no tuning" practical benefit.

Some CPPO baseline variants (e.g., CPPO-v1 in Appendix G) are acknowledged by the authors to perform very poorly, and the choice of which CPPO variant to report as "the" CPPO baseline in the main figures is not entirely clear, raising some concern about baseline framing.

The stochastic extension (SRABE) is only heuristically justified (interchanging extrema/expectation, acknowledged as an approximation without full guarantees), and the stochastic dynamics ablation is limited to a single environment (HalfCheetah) with only three seeds, limiting generality of the noise-robustness claims.

The generalization of decomposition principles beyond RAA/RR (e.g., to general nested temporal-logic-like specifications) is left entirely as future work, so the practical scope of the method remains restricted to these two specific compositions.

strengths: The theoretical core (Theorems 1 and 2) is substantial and carefully proven; the authors provide a full, rigorous derivation (spanning many appendix pages) showing that RAA and RR value functions can be decomposed into compositions of previously known Reach, Avoid, and Reach-Avoid value functions, including a non-trivial treatment of the need for state augmentation (Theorem 3) with a clean counterexample (Fig. 3) motivating why naive non-augmented policies fail.

The paper clearly differentiates its decomposition from superficially similar temporal-logic (TL) predicate algebra, explicitly showing (Appendix L) that TL quantitative-semantic decompositions do not translate into valid decompositions of the optimal HJ value functions, which is a useful clarification of the technical contribution's novelty.

The proposed DOHJ-PPO algorithm is grounded in the theory (SRABE/SRBE, coupled resets, concurrently trained decomposed and composed critics) and is evaluated against a fairly large and relevant set of baselines (Lagrangian/CPPO variants, HJ-RL baselines RESPO/RCPPO/RA, and STL/MORL-inspired baselines) across four distinct continuous-control domains (Hopper, F16, SafetyGym, HalfCheetah) for both RAA and RR tasks.

An additional stochastic-dynamics ablation (Fig. 5) is included to probe robustness of the SRBE/SRABE approximation (which interchanges extrema and expectation), which is an honest attempt to stress-test a known theoretical gap.
The qualitative DQN grid-world demonstration (Fig. 2) is a clear, interpretable illustration of how the RAA/RR values differ behaviorally from prior RA/R formulations.
weaknesses: There is a notable gap between theory and experiments: all theorems are proven for finite state/action MDPs with deterministic, known dynamics (explicitly stated in Section 3), yet the empirical evaluation is entirely on continuous-state, continuous-action, high-dimensional MuJoCo/aircraft/SafetyGym tasks with unknown dynamics learned via neural approximation. No formal argument bridges this gap, and the stochastic relaxation (SRABE) is explicitly acknowledged as unproven ("more work is needed to provide guarantees under stochastic dynamics"), leaving the core practical algorithm without solid theoretical backing in the exact regime it is deployed.

The reported results are presented almost entirely as qualitative bar-chart comparisons (Fig. 4-6) without numerical tables, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing across seeds for the main continuous-control results, making it hard to verify claims like "first or second place" or "increasingly dominates" quantitatively.

The construction of CPPO baselines reveals some cherry-picking: the authors describe trying three CPPO variants for RR and explicitly note that the "fairest" formulation (v1) performed worst while a "naive and seemingly unfair" variant (v3) was used because it outperformed the others, raising concerns about baseline tuning fairness and potential bias favoring the proposed method.

The method's scalability is questionable and explicitly flagged as future work: the approach to only two composite problems (RAA, RR) requires multiple additional actor/critic networks and coupled on-policy resets; the authors themselves state that generalizing to more complex logical compositions "would require deriving generalized decomposition principles" and a "more efficient representation," suggesting the current approach does not scale to richer task specifications despite motivating language about generalizing beyond R/A/RA.

Reward and penalty functions across all experimental domains are hand-crafted signed-distance functions to known geometric target/obstacle regions, which is a fairly narrow and favorable setting; it is unclear how the method performs with sparser, more realistic or learned reward signals, limiting the demonstrated generality of the "little to no tuning" claim.

The stochastic dynamics robustness study (Section 8.3) uses only three seeds and a single environment (HalfCheetah), which is a fairly limited ablation to support claims of general robustness to stochasticity.

The paper does not provide a reproducibility statement, code release, or link to released artifacts, which weakens confidence in the ability of the community to verify the extensive empirical claims given the many environment-specific reward engineering choices and hyperparameters (which vary notably between environments, e.g., different KP for CPPO across tasks).

strengths: Introduces two novel, well-motivated dual-objective problem formulations (RAA, RR) that meaningfully extend the existing HJ-RL framework (Reach, Avoid, Reach-Avoid) to compositional settings relevant for many practical safety/multi-goal tasks.

Provides rigorous theoretical results (Theorems 1-3 with full proofs in the appendix) establishing that RAA and RR value functions/optimal policies decompose into previously studied reach/avoid/reach-avoid value functions, and separately proves that the chosen state augmentation is sufficient for optimality.
Clear and convincing discussion (Section 5, Figure 3) of why naive non-augmented policies fail for these dual-objective tasks, which is an important and often overlooked subtlety.

Thorough and insightful comparison with temporal logic (TL) predicate decomposition in Appendix L, clarifying that algebraic decomposition at the specification level does not imply decomposition at the level of optimal value functions — a valuable theoretical contribution in its own right.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four diverse continuous-control domains (Hopper, F16, SafetyGym, HalfCheetah) against a large and relevant set of baselines (Lagrangian-based CPPO/PPO-Lag/P2BPO/LOGBAR, HJ-RL baselines RESPO/RCPPO/RA, and STL/MORL baselines), reporting success, partial success, and time-to-success metrics.

Additional robustness study under stochastic dynamics (Figure 5) with theoretical justification (SRBE/SRABE, Theorem 4) connecting deterministic decomposition results to a stochastic relaxation used in the practical algorithm.

The proposed DOHJ-PPO algorithm is a reasonably natural and well-justified extension of PPO, with clear ties back to the theoretical decomposition (coupled resets, concurrent decomposed/composed critics).
weaknesses: The approach is currently limited to compositions of exactly two objectives (RAA, RR); scaling to more objectives or arbitrary logical compositions is explicitly left as future work, limiting the generality claimed relative to full temporal-logic specifications.

The stochastic dynamics case lacks formal guarantees — the SRBE/SRABE substitution of expectation for extrema is only empirically validated and acknowledged as an approximation without a priori error bounds.

Baseline comparisons for the RR problem rely on multiple hand-crafted CPPO surrogate formulations (v1-v3) with highly variable performance, raising some concern about fairness/representativeness of the Lagrangian baselines and the effort invested in tuning them relative to DOHJ-PPO.

DOHJ-PPO is reported as achieving only 'first or second place' in Figure 4 rather than uniformly dominating, so the magnitude of improvement is somewhat environment-dependent and not universally decisive.

The paper is very dense, deferring almost all rigorous justification to a long appendix (25+ pages of proofs); while thorough, this limits self-containedness and makes independent verification by reviewers/readers more difficult within the main text.

Reward/penalty functions in the experiments are hand-designed per-environment (e.g., ad hoc signed-distance formulas), and it is unclear how sensitive performance is to these design choices or how the method would generalize to less-structured, learned reward specifications.
No explicit mention of code/data release, which raises mild reproducibility concerns despite detailed hyperparameter tables in the appendix.
